positions.commentary: The speaker questions if Amazon was strategic in letting Microsoft back in the game.
A Google engineer wrote a legendary post comparing Amazon and Google cultures, which went viral on Google+.
IBM had a business model of highly bundled hardware and software platforms with high margins, similar to Oracle and DEC.
Oracle had a business model of highly bundled hardware and software platforms with high margins, similar to IBM and DEC.
Netflix is still an enormous customer of AWS and Reed Hastings was the first guest interviewed on stage at re:Invent in 2012.
Airbnb was among the startups getting started in 2007-2008 and becoming big but not yet at today's scale.
Uber was among the startups getting started in 2007-2008 and becoming big but not yet at today's scale.
AWS makes 90+% gross margins on their bandwidth charges.

thesis: This episode argues that AWS won the most important market of all time by leveraging early scale and strategic relationships (like Netflix and the CIA), while competitors like Microsoft, Google, and Oracle failed to capture the cloud opportunity due to rigid business models, internal power struggles, or disruptive pricing issues. The thesis is thin because the provided claims focus heavily on historical failures of competitors and market share statistics rather than a cohesive forward-looking investment argument for AWS itself.

claims.claim: Microsoft was a decade early with Platform as a Service and failed to get startups or enterprises due to lack of mature platform and lift-and-shift ability.
claims.quote: The unfortunate thing for Microsoft and for Google, who really started at this Platform as a Service layer was, you basically didn't get the startups because you didn't have a mature platform yet that people were excited to build on and understood how to build for. But you also didn't get the enterprises because there was no ability to lift and shift.

claims.claim: Google was also a decade early with Platform as a Service and failed to get startups or enterprises for similar reasons as Microsoft.
claims.quote: The unfortunate thing for Microsoft and for Google, who really started at this Platform as a Service layer was, you basically didn't get the startups because you didn't have a mature platform yet that people were excited to build on and understood how to build for. But you also didn't get the enterprises because there was no ability to lift and shift.

I think what you're pointing out as these old server companies. The IBMs and Oracle on the database side, that made these ridiculous gross margins, and they sold you this complete proprietary solution.

claims.claim: Amazon has strong enterprise sales capabilities and a history of overcoming hurdles that Google faced, including migrating off Oracle databases.
claims.quote: Amazon didn't have to figure it out. But they then did also figure it out and served enterprises, governments, government agencies, big institutions, did the lift and shift thing, and then brought those big enterprises along.

claims.claim: Oracle's database market is huge, growing at 10% per year, and database software is the stickiest software of all time.

claims.claim: Amazon's Snowball and Snowmobile solutions help migrate data to the cloud, but it can still take six months to migrate all data.

claims.claim: Amazon.com took 13 years to migrate off Oracle databases after AWS launched.
claims.quote: Amazon.com used Oracle databases when it was started. Amazon.com did not finish their migration off of Oracle databases and onto AWS products until 2019.
